WITH character_keyword AS (SELECT id FROM keyword WHERE keyword = 'character-name-in-title')
SELECT MIN(n.name) AS member_in_charnamed_movie
FROM name AS n
JOIN cast_info AS ci ON n.id = ci.person_id
JOIN title AS t ON ci.movie_id = t.id
JOIN movie_keyword AS mk ON t.id = mk.movie_id AND mk.keyword_id = (SELECT id FROM character_keyword)
JOIN company_name AS cn ON (SELECT company_id FROM movie_companies WHERE movie_id = ci.movie_id) = cn.id
WHERE n.name LIKE '%B%' AND ci.movie_id = mk.movie_id

The query can be optimized by moving the subquery out of the WHERE clause and joining it as a table. This will reduce the number of times the subquery is evaluated. Here's the rewritten query:

```sql
WITH character_keyword AS (SELECT id FROM keyword WHERE keyword = 'character-name-in-title')
SELECT MIN(n.name) AS member_in_charnamed_movie
FROM name AS n
JOIN cast_info AS ci ON n.id = ci.person_id
JOIN title AS t ON ci.movie_id = t.id
JOIN movie_keyword AS mk ON t.id = mk.movie_id AND mk.keyword_id = (SELECT id FROM character_keyword)
JOIN company_name AS cn ON (SELECT company_id FROM movie_companies WHERE movie_id = ci.movie_id) = cn.id
WHERE n.name LIKE '%B%' AND ci.movie_id = mk.movie_id
```

This query creates a Common Table Expression (CTE) for the subquery, which is then joined like any other table. This should reduce the number of times the subquery is evaluated and improve performance.
